title: Moving into survivorship: long-term follow-up planning

guidelineVersions: NICE NG101: Early and locally advanced breast cancer (Published 18 July 2018; last updated 14 April 2025)
NICE CG164: Familial breast cancer (Published June 2013; last updated November 2023)

related.why: The most recent step in her treatment before this transition to survivorship
The original treatment plan this follow-up now completes

brief.setting: Breast clinic, one year after risk-reducing surgery, treatment complete
brief.scenario: Ms Linford, 45, has completed active treatment, including her mastectomy, radiotherapy, endocrine therapy, and risk-reducing gynaecological surgery. She is being discharged from frequent hospital follow-up into a long-term surveillance and self-monitoring plan.
brief.task: Discuss her ongoing follow-up plan and discharge from frequent clinic review. You have 7 minutes.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Frame this as a planned transition, not abandonment; be clear about what she needs to look out for and how to access help quickly if needed.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Presenting discharge from frequent follow-up as simply "good news" without checking how she feels about reduced hospital contact after such an intense period of treatment.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "How do you feel about the idea of fewer routine hospital appointments from here?"

flow: Check her feelings about reduced follow-up
Summarise the follow-up and surveillance plan
Explain symptoms that should prompt urgent contact
Discuss ongoing endocrine therapy adherence and side effects
Confirm access to support and closing

grid.label: Checking her feelings about discharge
grid.fail: Presents reduced follow-up purely as good news without checking her reaction.
grid.pass: Asks how she feels about fewer routine appointments before explaining the plan.
grid.high: Recognises that reduced hospital contact after intense treatment can feel unsettling as well as reassuring, without assuming either reaction.

grid.label: Explaining the surveillance plan
grid.fail: Cannot describe what ongoing follow-up will involve.
grid.pass: Explains the plan for ongoing mammographic surveillance and periodic review, and how this differs from her previous frequent appointments.
grid.high: Explains how her BRCA2 status specifically shapes her ongoing surveillance plan, distinct from standard post-treatment follow-up.

grid.label: Symptoms warranting urgent contact
grid.fail: Does not specify what symptoms should prompt her to seek review outside routine appointments.
grid.pass: Clearly lists symptoms that should prompt urgent contact, such as a new lump, unexplained pain, or systemic symptoms.
grid.high: Explains how she can access urgent review quickly (e.g. a direct contact route) rather than only through routine channels.

grid.label: Ongoing treatment and adherence
grid.fail: Does not check how she's getting on with ongoing endocrine therapy.
grid.pass: Asks about adherence and side effects of her ongoing endocrine therapy, and addresses any concerns raised.
grid.high: Explains why continued adherence matters even years into treatment, without being repetitive or patronising.

grid.label: Emotional check-in
grid.fail: Treats this purely as a logistical handover with no acknowledgement of her overall journey.
grid.pass: Acknowledges what she has been through over the past few years before moving to logistics.
grid.high: Checks in on her broader emotional wellbeing and offers ongoing psychological or peer support resources if wanted, without assuming she needs them.

grid.label: Access to support and closing
grid.fail: Ends without a clear point of contact if concerns arise.
grid.pass: Confirms how she can access the breast team quickly if something concerns her, even outside scheduled appointments.
grid.high: Provides written information summarising her follow-up plan and contact routes so she isn't relying on memory alone.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Good news, you're being discharged from regular follow-up now, so you won't need to come back as often.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: Oh. I didn't realise that was happening today.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's a good thing, don't worry. That's everything.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: How do you feel about the idea of fewer routine hospital appointments from here?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: A bit nervous, honestly, after so much contact with the team.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That's completely understandable. Your plan going forward is regular mammographic surveillance and periodic review, rather than the frequent visits you've had during active treatment.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: If you notice a new lump, unexplained pain, or feel generally unwell in a way that concerns you, you should contact us straight away rather than waiting for your next appointment.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: How are you getting on with your hormone tablets - any side effects or difficulty keeping up with them?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: You've been through an enormous amount these past few years, and it's worth acknowledging that before we finish today.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'll give you written details of your follow-up plan and how to contact us urgently if you ever need to.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: How does it feel, the idea of fewer routine hospital visits from here? I imagine that could feel like a relief, or maybe a bit unsettling, or both.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Honestly, both - relieved, but also a bit exposed without regular checks.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That makes complete sense. Going forward, your plan is regular mammographic surveillance and periodic review, tailored to your BRCA2 status rather than standard follow-up alone, so it is more than a generic discharge.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I want to be specific about what should bring you back urgently, outside routine appointments - a new lump, unexplained pain, weight loss, or anything that just doesn't feel right. And I'll give you a direct route to reach the team quickly, rather than going through general channels.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: How have you been getting on with your ongoing hormone therapy - any side effects, or difficulty keeping it up this far in?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: It's fine now, though it took a while to adjust.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Before we finish, I want to properly acknowledge everything you've been through these past few years - it's been a lot, and it's alright if stepping back from frequent contact feels strange even though it's a good sign clinically.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll give you written details of your plan and a direct contact route, so you're never relying on memory if you're worried about something.

failures.move: Presenting discharge from frequent follow-up purely as good news without checking her reaction.
failures.consequence: Misses that reduced contact after intense treatment can feel destabilising, not just reassuring, for many patients.

failures.move: Not specifying which symptoms should prompt urgent contact.
failures.consequence: Leaves her unsure when to seek help outside scheduled appointments, risking delayed presentation if something does arise.

failures.move: Treating this appointment as a purely administrative handover.
failures.consequence: Fails to acknowledge the scale of what she has been through, which can make the transition feel dismissive rather than supportive.

failures.move: Cannot describe what the follow-up surveillance plan actually involves.
failures.consequence: Leaves her without any concrete picture of what happens after discharge from frequent review.

failures.move: Never asks about her ongoing endocrine therapy or side effects.
failures.consequence: A missed opportunity to catch poor adherence or unmanaged side effects years into treatment.

recovery.when: You presented discharge as purely good news
recovery.line: I realise this might feel like a big change after so much contact with the team - how are you finding it?
Let me be specific about exactly what should bring you back to us urgently.

knowledge.fact: Following completion of active treatment, patients move to a surveillance and self-monitoring model of follow-up, with clear guidance on symptoms that should prompt urgent re-referral.
BRCA2 carriers require tailored ongoing surveillance distinct from standard post-treatment follow-up.
Adherence to adjuvant endocrine therapy remains important throughout its full prescribed duration, which is typically several years.

recall.think: Discharge from frequent review can feel unsettling, not just reassuring; be specific about red flags; acknowledge the journey, don't just hand over logistics.
recall.say: "I imagine that could feel like a relief, or maybe a bit unsettling, or both."
do: Check her feelings about reduced follow-up before explaining the plan
Give specific red-flag symptoms and access to urgent review, and check endocrine therapy adherence
Acknowledge her overall journey before closing on logistics

numbers.meaning: minimum duration of adjuvant endocrine therapy, continuing through this follow-up transition

recall.trap: Framing discharge from frequent follow-up as unambiguously good news without checking how it actually feels to her.
recall.finish: A clear, tailored surveillance plan, specific red-flag guidance, a direct contact route, and her overall journey acknowledged.

partner.opening: Please discuss this patient's transition to long-term follow-up and discharge from frequent review. You have 7 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Rachel Linford, 45, a year after your risk-reducing surgery, treatment complete. You feel both relieved and anxious about fewer hospital visits after such an intense few years, and want to know exactly what to watch for and how to get help quickly if needed.

reveals.trigger: Candidate checks how you feel about reduced follow-up
reveals.finding: You admit to feeling both relieved and a bit exposed.

reveals.trigger: Candidate gives specific, memorable red-flag symptoms
reveals.finding: You feel reassured knowing exactly what to look out for.
You become visibly moved, appreciating being seen beyond the logistics.

push.question: What exactly should make me come back urgently?
push.expect: Give specific, concrete red-flag symptoms and a direct route to urgent review.

push.question: What if I just feel anxious even without a specific symptom?
push.expect: Acknowledge this as valid and offer psychological or peer support resources without dismissing the anxiety as unfounded.

curveballs.prompt: I still check myself for lumps every single day, is that normal?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Normalise vigilance after everything she's experienced, while gently discussing whether daily checking feels helpful or is adding to anxiety, and offering support if it's the latter.

curveballs.prompt: What if I forget everything you've just told me?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Reassure her that written information will be provided summarising the plan and contact details, so she doesn't need to rely on memory alone.
